subject: biology
title: Testing for biological molecules and chromatography
key_idea: Chemical tests identify sugars, starch, lipids and protein by a colour change or an emulsion. Comparing a test with standards of known concentration gives an estimate of concentration. Chromatography separates mixtures by how far each solute moves.

blocks.text: Each test uses a reagent that changes in a recognisable way when a particular molecule is present.

rows: Add Benedict's solution to the sample. Heat in a water bath at about 80 °C for several minutes.
Blue to green, yellow, orange, then brick-red precipitate
Add iodine in potassium iodide solution to the sample.
Shake the sample with ethanol. Pour the mixture into water.
Add sodium hydroxide, then dilute copper(II) sulfate solution.

diagram.alt: Pick a food sample and see the result of the Benedict's, iodine, biuret and emulsion tests on it.

options.label: Sucrose solution
options.explanation: Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar, so the Benedict's test is negative until it is hydrolysed with acid.

options.label: Distilled water
options.explanation: Water is the negative control: it shows what each reagent looks like when nothing is present.

items: Benedict's detects reducing sugars (brick-red), iodine detects starch (blue-black).
Biuret detects protein (purple); the emulsion test detects lipid (cloudy white).
A negative control with water shows the reagent's starting colour.

blocks.text: Sucrose does not reduce Benedict's solution. It must first be hydrolysed to release reducing sugars.

items.text: Do a Benedict's test on the sample. It stays blue, so there is no reducing sugar.
Boil a fresh sample with dilute hydrochloric acid. The acid breaks the glycosidic bond.
Add sodium hydrogencarbonate until the fizzing stops. Benedict's solution only works in alkaline conditions.
Heat with Benedict's solution. A brick-red precipitate shows a non-reducing sugar was present.

items: Negative before hydrolysis and positive after: a non-reducing sugar.
Positive before hydrolysis: a reducing sugar was already present.

blocks.text: Colour tests can be made semi-quantitative. The result for an unknown is compared with results for known concentrations.

items: Make a **serial dilution** of a stock solution to give a range of known concentrations (standards), for example by halving the concentration each time.
**Standardise** the test: use the same volume of reagent and sample, the same temperature and the same heating time each time.
Test the unknown in the same way and compare it with the standards.
Repeat each test and use a negative control, so that any difference is due to concentration.
Standards of known concentration are made by serial dilution.
Every variable except concentration is kept the same.

checks.q: A solution gives no colour change with Benedict's solution. After boiling with dilute acid, neutralising and heating with Benedict's solution it gives a brick-red precipitate. What does this show, and why?
checks.a: It contains a non-reducing sugar, such as sucrose. Acid hydrolysis broke the glycosidic bond and released reducing sugars, which give a positive Benedict's test.

checks.q: Describe how to test a solution for protein and state the positive result.
checks.a: Add sodium hydroxide, then dilute copper(II) sulfate solution (biuret reagent) and mix. A purple (lilac) colour shows protein is present; it stays blue if not.

checks.q: Why is a serial dilution used when estimating the concentration of a reducing sugar?
checks.a: It gives a series of standard solutions of known concentration to compare with the unknown. The unknown's concentration is estimated from the standard it matches.

items: **Standardise** the test: same volumes of sample and Benedict's solution, same water bath temperature, same type of tube.
Method 1: measure the **time to the first colour change**. The higher the concentration, the shorter the time.
Method 2: compare the colour after a fixed time with **colour standards** made from known concentrations. The more concentrated the sugar, the further the colour moves towards brick-red.
Use the results from the standards to estimate the concentration of the unknown.
A **colorimeter** measures how much light a coloured solution absorbs. Absorbance rises with concentration.
Use a filter whose colour is complementary to the solution, so the solution absorbs it strongly.
Set the colorimeter to zero using a blank of the solvent, usually water, or the reagent without the test substance.
Measure the absorbance of the standards from a serial dilution. Plot a **calibration curve** of absorbance against concentration.
Measure the unknown and read its concentration from the curve.

items.meaning: The paper, or the thin layer of silica or cellulose on a plate, which holds still.
The solvent that moves up the stationary phase and carries the solutes.
The highest point the solvent reaches.

items: Different solutes dissolve in the solvent to different extents and stick to the stationary phase to different extents.
A solute that is more soluble in the solvent, and less attracted to the stationary phase, travels further.
Chromatography separates biological molecules such as amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins and nucleic acids.

items.text: Draw a pencil line near the bottom. Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent.
Put small, concentrated spots of each sample on the line, and a spot of known compounds to compare.
Stand the paper or plate in a covered container with solvent below the baseline. Let the solvent rise.
Remove it before the solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front at once.
Many biological molecules are colourless, so spray with a locating agent such as ninhydrin for amino acids, or use UV light.

blocks.label: Rf value
blocks.formula: Rf = distance moved by the solute ÷ distance moved by the solvent
where: Both distances are measured from the baseline, in the same unit.
Rf has no unit and is always between 0 and 1.

diagram.alt: Calculate an Rf value from a solute distance and a solvent distance.
diagram.question: A spot moves {solute} mm from the baseline. The solvent front moves {solvent} mm. Calculate the Rf value.
working: Rf = distance moved by solute ÷ distance moved by solvent.

items: Identify a substance by matching its Rf value to the Rf of a known compound in the same solvent.
Thin layer chromatography usually separates faster and gives sharper spots than paper chromatography.
